paragraphs.heading: A solid ball at the center
paragraphs.text: Earth's inner core is the deepest layer of the planet. It is mostly a solid ball roughly 1,230 km in radius, about a fifth of Earth's radius and seven tenths of the Moon's. Scientists think it is an alloy of iron and nickel mixed with some other elements. Its surface is estimated at around 5,700 K, close to the temperature at the surface of the Sun. It stays solid in spite of that heat because the pressure on it is so high.

paragraphs.heading: Learning about a place no one can reach
paragraphs.text: Nobody can collect a sample of the core, unlike the mantle. What we know comes mostly from seismic waves, such as those sent out by deep earthquakes, and from Earth's magnetic field. Almost every measurement of the inner core's physical properties comes from seismic waves that pass through it. These come in two main kinds. P waves, or pressure waves, compress the material and can cross both solids and liquids, while S waves, or shear waves, can move only through rigid solids.

paragraphs.heading: Inge Lehmann's discovery
paragraphs.text: In 1936 the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann studied records of earthquakes in New Zealand and found that Earth has a solid inner core separate from its molten outer core. She reasoned that seismic waves were bouncing off the inner core's edge and estimated its radius at 1,400 km, close to the value of 1,221 km accepted today. In 1938 Beno Gutenberg and Charles Richter, using more data, placed its radius between 1,230 and 1,530 km. In 1952 Francis Birch concluded that it was probably crystalline iron, and its rigidity was confirmed in 1971.

paragraphs.heading: Waves that prove it is solid
paragraphs.text: S waves cannot travel into or out of the inner core as they are. But when a P wave hits the boundary between the inner and outer core at a slant, it can turn into an S wave, and the reverse can happen too. Waves known as PKJKP make exactly this switch: they cross the inner core as S waves and become P waves again on the way out. Because the inner core can carry S waves, it must be solid. Researchers also study PKiKP waves, which bounce off the inner core's surface, and PKIKP waves, which pass through it.

paragraphs.heading: Size and shape
paragraphs.text: Seismic data put the radius at about 1,221 km, roughly 19% of Earth's radius. Its volume, about 7.6 billion cubic km, is only around 0.69% of the volume of the whole planet. Its shape is thought to be slightly squashed, like Earth's, but rounder. Its radius along Earth's axis is about 3 km shorter than its radius at the equator, while for the whole Earth that gap is 21 km.

paragraphs.heading: Crushing conditions
paragraphs.text: The pressure inside the inner core ranges from about 330 to 360 gigapascals, or 3.3 to 3.6 million atmospheres. Gravity at its surface works out to 4.3 m/s², less than half of the 9.8 m/s² at Earth's surface. Its density is about 13.0 kg/L at the center and falls gradually to about 12.8 kg/L at its outer edge. Just above it, in the liquid outer core, the density drops suddenly to about 12.1 kg/L.

paragraphs.heading: Still full of surprises
paragraphs.text: Signs reported as recently as February 2025 suggest the inner core may be partly deformable, not the fully solid sphere it was long believed to be. It also matters for Earth's magnetic field. That field seems to come mostly from fluid and electric currents in the outer core, but the solid inner core and the heat flowing out of it strongly affect those currents.
